[4] # Preliminary incident report: DSV Cormorant, dive 214

Filed by the Dive Operations Officer, 3 November. At 09:42 local time on 2 November, the deep submergence vehicle Cormorant
departed the support ship Halvard Lyng for a routine survey of the Kestrel Rise,
a basalt ridge in the eastern basin. The dive plan called for four hours at a
working depth of 1,850 metres, with two hours of transit either side. Aboard
were pilot Ines Okonkwo, co-pilot Tobias Reiner, and observer Dr Amara Sell. Descent was normal. At 11:14, passing 1,610 metres, the vehicle reported a
transient dropout on the primary power bus lasting approximately 400
milliseconds. The crew logged it and continued.

just over two seconds and took the forward thrusters and the primary lighting
array offline. Both recovered without intervention. At 11:58, at a depth of 1,844 metres, the primary bus failed entirely. The
vehicle transferred to the reserve bus as designed. The reserve bus carries life
support, communications, and the ballast release, but not propulsion. Cormorant
was at that point neutrally buoyant and drifting at approximately 0.3 knots on
the prevailing current. The crew followed the standard procedure and released the descent weights at
12:04. Ascent began at roughly 22 metres per minute. Cormorant surfaced at 13:31
approximately 4.1 nautical miles east of the Halvard Lyng and was recovered at
14:52.

[6] Cormorant surfaced at 13:31
approximately 4.1 nautical miles east of the Halvard Lyng and was recovered at
14:52. No injuries were sustained. Dr Sell reported a headache consistent with
the elevated carbon dioxide observed in the final forty minutes of ascent. The vehicle was recovered intact. Initial inspection found no hull breach and no
water ingress in the pressure sphere. The cause of the bus failure was not
determined at the time of filing and is referred to Engineering. This report is preliminary. It records what was observed and does not attempt to

0b67521d4cf12094509a4906f893a9e7d3088de5.text: Based on the incident report, the crew's actions during the dive itself appear to have been appropriate. They logged the transient dropouts and continued as permitted by the procedures they were given. However, the pilot's own assessment suggests a systemic problem rather than crew error: she noted that "the criteria are wrong" and that "we were given two warnings and told we did not need to listen." The investigation found that the abort criteria they were operating under did not adequately account for the types of failures that occurred. So while the crew followed their instructions, the real mistake appears to have been in the procedures and safety criteria established before the dive, not in how the crew executed it.

ridge wall.

We are seeing the thermocline as a shimmer rather than a wall. 1114. Sixteen ten. We had a flicker on the main bus, under half a second. Everything came back on its own. Logged it. Tobias says he has seen worse on the
older vehicles. Continuing. 1131. Sixteen ten again, holding for the survey line. Second flicker and this
one had teeth — two seconds, and it took the forward thrusters and the main
lights with it.

warnings, which is why two warnings produced no obligation. The board endorses all three of the Engineering recommendations and adds a
fourth: that abort criteria be reviewed by someone outside the operating group,
annually.

Based on the engineering findings, three key changes are recommended:

First, penetrator seal replacement work should be restricted to shore facilities rather than performed at sea, since the wet bay is not a clean environment and a hard particle trapped during the August maintenance period caused the failure.

48f94eb4eb873a8f1042089f0832f95eed28cd03.text: The Cormorant lost power due to a failure in the starboard bus junction caused by a scored penetrator seat that admitted seawater. Salt deposits accumulated at the junction over time, raising electrical resistance until the bus ultimately failed. This occurred about twenty-seven minutes after two earlier warning transients, the second of which had briefly taken propulsion offline at 1,610 metres depth.

facility, following the schedule compression agreed after the Kestrel Rise
survey was brought forward. Seal replacement at sea is permitted under the
maintenance manual. It is performed in the wet bay, which is not a clean
environment. Recommendations. First, penetrator seal work should be restricted to the shore
facility. Second, any transient on the primary bus exceeding one second should
be a mandatory abort. Third, the reserve bus should carry sufficient power for
station-keeping, so that a vehicle on reserve is not obliged to surface blind
under whatever current it happens to be in.

without thrusters — you go up where the water takes you. 1452. Aboard. Everyone walked out.

compression seal deformed into the scoring, opening a path for seawater to reach
the conductor.

[5] # Preliminary incident report: DSV Cormorant, dive 214

Filed by the Dive Operations Officer, 3 November. At 09:42 local time on 2 November, the deep submergence vehicle Cormorant
departed the support ship Halvard Lyng for a routine survey of the Kestrel Rise,
a basalt ridge in the eastern basin. The dive plan called for four hours at a
working depth of 1,850 metres, with two hours of transit either side. Aboard
were pilot Ines Okonkwo, co-pilot Tobias Reiner, and observer Dr Amara Sell. Descent was normal. At 11:14, passing 1,610 metres, the vehicle reported a
transient dropout on the primary power bus lasting approximately 400
milliseconds. The crew logged it and continued.

Finally, the reserve bus should carry sufficient power for station-keeping so that a vehicle operating on reserve power is not forced to surface blind under whatever current conditions exist.

technicians, signed off the same day. The maintenance manual requires visual
inspection of the seat before the new seal is fitted. That inspection is
recorded as performed. The manual does not require the seat to be measured, and

[2] The August maintenance period was carried out at sea rather than in the shore
facility, following the schedule compression agreed after the Kestrel Rise
survey was brought forward. Seal replacement at sea is permitted under the
maintenance manual. It is performed in the wet bay, which is not a clean
environment. Recommendations. First, penetrator seal work should be restricted to the shore
facility. Second, any transient on the primary bus exceeding one second should
be a mandatory abort. Third, the reserve bus should carry sufficient power for
station-keeping, so that a vehicle on reserve is not obliged to surface blind
under whatever current it happens to be in.

[3] # Engineering findings: primary bus failure, DSV Cormorant

To the Dive Operations Officer, 19 November. From the Vehicle Systems group. We have completed teardown of the primary power distribution assembly recovered
from dive 214. The failure originated in the starboard penetrator block, at the
junction where the main bus passes from the pressure sphere into the wet bay. The penetrator uses a compression seal against a machined titanium seat. On
disassembly we found the seat scored along roughly a third of its circumference. The scoring is consistent with a hard particle trapped during the seal
replacement carried out in the August maintenance period. Under pressure the
compression seal deformed into the scoring, opening a path for seawater to reach
the conductor.
